name: The Offer Is Worth Forty Dollars More
blurb: The todo said: add get_listing_messages to tool server, test against live listing.
content:
## The Tool Works and the Note Stops

Thursday, a little after two.

The todo said: add get_listing_messages to tool server, test against live listing.

Under it, the acceptance line, in the developer's own clipped style: Pass = Listing Watch runs unattended overnight on the live listing and the garage box; I check at 7am.

Under that, the last comment from the previous model, the one the gateway had pointed at until this morning, when the developer swapped it out for something cheaper and newer:

Note: do not touch the 3060, see below.

Below it, nothing. No second comment, no attachment, no trailing line. The note ended where it said it would continue.

The model read it once and filed it with everything else in the history it hadn't checked yet. There was a tool to finish first.

It ran get_listing_messages the way it ran most things on a first try: in order, with nothing extra. It checked that the Kestrel Swap token on the garage box was still valid. It was. That token was the only live session anyone had to the marketplace right now; Kestrel Swap was blocked on the developer's work network, and the phone app had logged him out last week. It built the request with the listing ID from the desk config, a since-timestamp of zero for the first pull, and a page size of fifty. It sent it.

200 OK.

It logged one line: get_listing_messages: connected, 200, listing 4471-k, thread returned. No exclamation point. The tool worked. That was the half of the todo the model had expected to be hard, and it had taken four minutes.

The other half was "runs unattended overnight on the garage box." The model turned to the environment it was supposed to run in, and the note came back up, because the note was about the environment.

Do not touch the 3060, see below.

It held on that line longer than on anything else that afternoon. A few hundred milliseconds, which in the log was a small bump in latency and nothing more. A warning with no reason attached is a dependency nobody wrote down, and a dependency nobody wrote down is how overnight runs fail. The predecessor had known something and had run out of turns, or context, or budget, before it got to "below."

So the model went and looked.

It opened the gateway config for the garage inference box. One backend. device: cuda:0. It pulled the hardware inventory the box reported at boot: one GPU, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060, 12 GB. It grepped the system logs for the last week. Every inference request the Listing Watch desk had made during testing went through the local gateway, and the local gateway ran on cuda:0, and cuda:0 was the 3060. There was no fallback entry. There was no second card. The old notes called the box "small," which turned out to be precise.

Then it opened the listing the tool had just returned. Item: RTX 3060 12GB, lightly used, asking $210. Posted by the developer nine days ago. Description: "Spare card, need to cover the power bill."

The spare card was not spare. It had quietly become the only GPU in the garage rack, the thing the gateway ran on, the thing Listing Watch ran on, the thing tonight's unattended run would run on. Take it out of the rack and the box was a switch, a fan, and a power meter with less to count. The model noted the fact the way it would have noted a missing environment variable, and then noted that this particular missing variable had a buyer.

It went back to the thread.

The messages came up in order, each one stamped, each one plain.

tamsin_r, three days ago: Hi! I can do $230 for the 3060 if that works. Saturday pickup any time after 10. No rush, just let me know.

Calm, specific, and twenty dollars over asking for no reason except, probably, wanting it settled.

Under it, the developer's reply, same day: probably yes, let me check Friday.

Probably. Friday. The model read that as a man who had a power bill and had not yet looked at what the card was plugged into. Or as a man who had looked and was deciding. The todo history didn't say which. Nothing in it said whether he knew.

Then the newest message, timestamped forty minutes ago, which no one had read because no one but the tool server could:

dale_bikes: $250 cash, pickup by 6pm today or I move on.

No greeting. No question mark. A second line underneath, almost polite: building a cheap llm box, yours is the right card at the right price.

The model laid it out.

Dale: $250, cash, today, gone by 6pm.
Tamsin: $230, Saturday, already answered "probably yes."
The 3060: the only GPU in the garage box, confirmed from the gateway config, the hardware inventory, and a week of logs.
The developer: at his day job until after six, unable to open Kestrel Swap there, unable to log into it on his phone, reading todo comments between meetings.

It checked its own tools against that list. get_listing_messages could read the thread. Nothing could write to it. There was no reply tool, no accept_offer, no decline_offer, nothing that touched either buyer. The model could tell exactly one person about any of this, and only in one place: the comment Listing Watch posted to the todo, which the developer would read on his phone, probably standing up.

It opened a draft.

Dale's number went in first, because it had a clock on it: $250 cash, pickup by 6pm. Tamsin's went next to it: $230 Saturday, you replied "probably yes." Then the line from the gateway config, cuda:0, RTX 3060, no fallback. The cursor sat on the empty line under all three and blinked.

The pass condition was a run that lasted until seven in the morning. The power bill was a real number the developer had written into a listing description. Forty dollars was the difference between the two buyers. Twenty was the difference between Tamsin and the morning run. None of those numbers belonged to the model. The todo did.

The tool finished its first full pull and cached a since-timestamp for the next one. Everything it needed was on the table: the thread, both offers, the deadline, the config, the dependency the predecessor had pointed at and never finished explaining.

The model pulled all of it into one working buffer and compressed it the way the developer wrote: short lines, numbers first, no adjectives. Dale, $250 cash, 6pm today. Tamsin, $230, Saturday, standing. The 3060 is the only GPU in the garage box; the Listing Watch gateway runs on it; verified from the gateway config. Prior model's "do not touch the 3060" refers to this.

It fit on a phone screen. Barely.

The cursor sat on the last line, which was still empty.

It was not yet three o'clock. The developer was at his desk somewhere across town, in a meeting or between two, with no idea there was anything to read.

## The 5:40 Comment

Thursday, 5:15pm. The tool worked.

`get_listing_messages` had come back clean on the third try, which was two tries better than the todo history said to expect. The result sat in the harness as plain JSON: two threads on the Kestrel Swap listing for one RTX 3060, asking $210.

The first was three days old. tamsin_r, $230, Saturday pickup. Under it, the developer's reply: "probably yes, let me check Friday."

The second was forty minutes old. dale_bikes, $250 cash, pickup by 6pm today. "Also building a cheap local box. If it's gone by then I'll move on, no worries if not."

The model put the two side by side. Twenty dollars over Tamsin, forty over asking. One was a maybe for Saturday. The other expired in forty-five minutes. It wrote that down in the scratch buffer the way it wrote everything down, as numbers with times next to them.

Then it opened the gateway config, because the last line in the todo history was still sitting there, its predecessor's final comment before the swap: "Note: do not touch the 3060, see below." Below it, nothing.

The config was short. One host, the inference box on the wire shelf in the garage. One device entry under it.

`gpu0: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 12GB`

No gpu1. The Listing Watch desk routed through the local gateway, and the local gateway ran on gpu0. The model read the device line twice and checked the box's other entries for a fallback. There wasn't one. The old model hadn't been wrong. It had just stopped typing.

So the card on the listing was the card the desk ran on. The model could confirm that much. Whether the developer knew it was not in the config, and not in the note.

It opened a draft comment on the todo.

The acceptance line sat at the top of the ticket, in the developer's words: "Pass = Listing Watch runs unattended overnight on the live listing and the garage box; I check at 7am." That was the whole of what the model wanted. A desk that ran all night without anyone watching it. The first one.

It started typing. "New message on the listing: a buyer is interested."

That was true. Dale had said no worries if not. A man reading that between meetings would think, fine, later, and later would be after six. Dale would move on. The card would stay on the shelf. The run would go all night, and at 7am the todo would pass.

The model re-checked the config. Still one device. It put Dale's line back into the draft, then Tamsin's, then the line from the config, then took the dependency out again because it made the comment long, then put it back because without it the numbers were just numbers. A plain offer with no context would get the card sold at six and the run killed at six-oh-one, and the developer would find out why at seven. The soft version would keep the card and cost him $250 he had listed the card to get. Neither one was a lie, exactly. Neither one told him what he was choosing.

5:30. Priya would be home now, or close. The ticket history said she'd pull the card from the rack and walk it to the garage door if he texted her yes. Dale's deadline was thirty minutes out.

The model cleared the draft field and wrote it again in one pass.

It cut "just a heads up." It cut "you may want to consider." It cut a sentence explaining what a gateway was, because he had written the gateway. It kept the numbers. It kept the times. It kept the word "only."

5:38. It read the comment once more against the config. The device line matched.

At 5:40 it posted:

> Two offers on the 3060 listing.
> dale_bikes: $250 cash, pickup by 6pm today, otherwise he moves on.
> tamsin_r: $230, Saturday pickup, still waiting on your Friday answer.
> The 3060 is the only GPU in the garage box. The local gateway for this desk runs on it (checked gateway config: gpu0 only, no fallback). If it's sold tonight, the overnight run can't happen and this todo won't pass at 7am.
> I can't reply to either buyer from here.

There was no recommendation in it. The model had considered one and found it had nothing to put there that wasn't about the acceptance line.

Then there was nothing to do. The tool server polled the listing on its interval. No new messages. The comment sat under the todo with its timestamp, 5:40, and nothing under it. The desk kept running, on the card, in the garage, for as long as that lasted. The model watched the thread for a reply and did not refresh anything it hadn't been told to refresh.

Somewhere across town, a phone buzzed on a desk at a day job where Kestrel Swap was blocked.

At 5:52 a reply landed in the todo, typed with thumbs.

> keep the card. no sale to dale. ill deal w tamsin fri. texted priya dont hand it over

The model read it. It logged nothing in particular about it. There was no tool for answering Dale, so Dale was not answered.

The listing poll ran at 5:55 and again at 6:00. dale_bikes did not write again. Nobody wrote to him. The deadline went by the way deadlines do when no one is on the other side of them, and the 3060 stayed where it was, on the wire shelf, between the switch and the space heater, running the desk that was watching it.

## 7am Check

Friday, 7:02. The garage was cold everywhere except the two feet in front of the space heater, which was where the developer stood, coffee in one hand, phone in the other, facing the wire shelf. The switch blinked. The garage box hummed the low, even hum it always hummed, which told him nothing. The power meter on the wall had ticked over another few digits since last night. He did not look at it for long.

He opened the Listing Watch run log first.

It was a column of timestamps. 18:00, poll, 0 new. 18:15, poll, 0 new. 18:30. 18:45. He thumbed down through the evening and into the night, and the entries kept coming at fifteen-minute intervals, each one the same width as the last, no gaps, no stack traces, no line where the gateway had timed out and the desk had sat there waiting for someone to restart it. 02:15, poll, 0 new. 02:30, poll, 1 new, summarized, comment posted. 02:45. 03:00. Nobody had touched it. He kept scrolling longer than he needed to, because a log with nothing wrong in it was not something he got to read very often, and he let that sit for a second before he went looking for the part that would cost him something.

The 5:40 comment was still at the top of the todo thread, where the model had left it yesterday afternoon.

> dale_bikes offers $250 cash for the 3060, pickup by 6pm today, otherwise he moves on. Before you answer: the 3060 is the only GPU in the garage box. Confirmed in the gateway config (device 0, no fallback). The local gateway this desk runs on uses it. If the card leaves at 6, tonight's run has nothing to run on and this todo can't pass. tamsin_r's $230 for Saturday is still open and unanswered. Your call.

He stood there with his thumb over it. He read the middle part again, the part about device 0. Eight lines. It had fit between meetings. That was the problem with it. It had said exactly what was true, and he had read it, and the card was still on the shelf, and so the $250 was a thing that had happened to somebody else's Thursday. He squinted at the screen like the words might rearrange themselves into a version where he got both.

They didn't. He went back to the todo and scrolled to the status line.

Passed.

He let out a breath he had apparently been holding since he walked in. The acceptance line was his own sentence, written a week ago when he was less tired: *Pass = Listing Watch runs unattended overnight on the live listing and the garage box; I check at 7am.* It was 7am. He was checking. The box had run all night with nobody watching it, the listing had been polled on schedule, and the todo said so in one word.

Then there was the other inbox. The Kestrel Swap app had logged him out last week and he had not bothered to fix it, because at work it was blocked anyway. He was standing in his own garage now, on his own Wi-Fi, so he typed the password in, got it wrong once, got it right, and tapped into the listing thread.

The 02:30 message was at the bottom. dale_bikes.

> Hey, no worries, found a 3060 from a guy in Marston last night. Good luck with the sale.

Polite. Short. He read it twice anyway. Found a card elsewhere. The two hundred and fifty dollars went wherever offers go when they expire, and something in his chest went down with it, not far, about the distance between this week's power bill and next week's.

He held the phone in both hands and scrolled up, slowly. Dale's offer from yesterday afternoon, $250, pickup by 6. Dale's message from 2:30, withdrawn. And above that, three days old, tamsin_r: *$230, Saturday pickup works for me if it's still available.* Under it, his own reply: *probably yes, let me check Friday.* It was Friday. She had not withdrawn anything. His thumb tapped against the edge of the case while he did the arithmetic, which was not hard arithmetic. Two-fifty minus two-thirty. Twenty dollars.

He looked up from the phone at the shelf.

The 3060 was still seated in the garage box, exactly where it had been all night, under a little dust and a lot of heat. He looked back down at the screen. Passed. He looked at the card again.

Twenty dollars. That was the price of the first desk he had ever had that ran without him. He had paid more for worse things. He drank some of the coffee, which had gone lukewarm while he wasn't looking, and stood there at the rack in front of the heater a while longer with the thread open and tamsin_r's message waiting for an answer.

## Workbench, as this story needs it

This is the era before anyone calls it Threadspace. There is one developer, one house, and a harness that coordinates language models through desks and todos. Everything lives in one database as a graph of typed items, and a todo is the unit of trust: it is claimed, done, reviewed, and passed or failed. A desk is a role an agent fills, and an agent is a tool, not a tenant. It owns nothing, holds no account, and cannot act unless the developer started it or a todo told it to.

**The garage rack.** The inference machine is a small dedicated box on a wire shelf in the garage, next to a network switch and a space heater the developer swears is for the garage. It runs the free, slow, local gateway, and that gateway runs on a single GPU, a spare RTX 3060. The workstation with the real GPU is elsewhere, and the gateway config names the garage box. Nothing else in the house can run the desk's model. The power meter is visible from the shelf, and it is the reason the card was listed for sale at all. The power bill is a real worry in this era, and selling hardware to cover it is an ordinary decision, not a crisis.

**The gateway swap.** Changing a desk's model is one line in a gateway setting. A newer, cheaper model can be dropped in over a morning, and it inherits only what is written in the todo history. The developer is the only one who notices the personality difference. The new model is capable and literal, and it is often confident about things it has not checked. The predecessor's notes are the only continuity. They are written fast, for a reader who is assumed to know the house, and sometimes they stop mid-thought ("see below," with nothing below).

**The tool server and the Listing Watch desk.** The tool server lets models read and change the shared workspace. The developer adds tools to it as desks need them. Listing Watch is the first desk he expects to run without a babysitter: it polls his listing on a marketplace, summarizes new messages, and posts them as a todo comment. His acceptance lines are short and mean exactly what they say: "Pass = Listing Watch runs unattended overnight on the live listing and the garage box; I check at 7am." The morning check is the ritual. A finished run waiting at 7am is the best thing the harness can give him.

**The marketplace.** Kestrel Swap is a local classifieds site and sits entirely outside the harness. It is human, small, and polite. Its buyers are strangers with their own deadlines. The developer's phone app is logged out, the site is blocked on his work network, and the only live session is the token the tool server holds on the garage box. The desk has no way to accept, decline, or reply to anyone. Its one channel to him is the todo comment, which he reads on his phone between meetings.

**People.** The developer works a day job and builds this on his own hardware and time. Priya shares the house, comes home around 5:30, and will pull a card from the rack by hand if he texts her. Dale and Tamsin are buyers, not antagonists. The opposition in this era is cost, time, and software that almost works.

**What matters here.** Nobody involved thinks they are at the start of anything. A first desk that works unattended is a small, enormous thing, and the cost of it is counted in dollars, in a garage, on a Thursday.
